newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Kids paid $22 a month to stitch soccer balls.
newsitem.headline: Kids paid $22 a month to stitch soccer balls.

text.p: At least 14,700 children aged seven to 14 work full time in one Pakistani city stitching soccer balls and filing surgical instruments, earning less than the minimum wage, a survey released on Sunday said.
The survey of Sialkot, centre of the Pakistani sports goods industry, was carried out by the International Labour Organisation (ILO) and Pakistan's labour authorities.
It followed a survey by the Labour Ministry in collaboration with the ILO in October which said 3.6 million children aged five to 14 were working full time in Pakistan.

Pakistan, faced with scathing international criticism and threats of trade sanctions, has taken steps to curb child labour, but officials say total elimination is impossible in a country where poverty and illiteracy are rife.
In 1990, Pakistan ratified the U.N. Convention on the Rights of the Child that prohibits child labour, but legal experts say more legislation needs to be enacted to implement it.

"Children are mainly involved in the stitching of footballs and filing of surgical instruments, the most labour-intensive and time-consuming phase in the manufacturing process," said the survey on Sialkot.

"It is estimated that 7,000 child workers were involved in football stitching on a regular and full-time basis (17 percent of the workforce in soccer ball stitching) with an additional large number of children involved on a part-time basis outside of school hours," said the study, carried out in 1996.

The survey said the surgical instruments industry employed about 7,700 children, or 31 percent of its total workforce. Six percent of them were involved in grinding and polishing, hazardous occupations due to high metal dust levels.

Average monthly earnings were 886 rupees ($22) for skilled children making soccer balls and 1,300 rupees ($32) for children making surgical instruments, against the minimum wage of 1,650 rupees ($41) set by the government for adult unskilled workers.
"The children's daily working hours were found to be eight to nine hours in football stitching and eight hours in surgical instrument making," the survey added.

It said the children grinding and polishing instruments were involved in work that was "clearly dangerous" to them, but the other children did not face major safety and health problems, except for needle injuries, and abrasions during filing.
The survey said Pakistan exported 20 million soccer balls to European and American markets in 1995 against 35 million in 1993 when demand was high due to the World Cup football tournament.
The survey is part of a programme to eliminate "hazardous and exploitative" child labour in the border city of Sialkot.
The unregulated piecework system, with no checks on child labour, is under threat from international pressure that has prompted some multinational sports goods firms to take action.
